prompt: Discuss Aristotle's account of phantasia and its role in practical reasoning, drawing on De Anima III.3 and the relevant commentators.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis Aristotle's account of φαντασία in *De Anima* III.3 is situated at the decisive juncture between his treatment of sense-perception (αἴσθησις) and his investigation of intellect (νοῦς), such that phantasia emerges as a mediating capacity irreducible to either faculty. As White observes, Aristotle's treatment of phantasia occurs "at a critical juncture between his account of sensation and his account of nous," positioning it as a conceptual hinge upon which the architecture of the soul's cognitive operations turns (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). This passage crystallizes the fundamental contrast: whereas αἴσθησις requires the actual presence of an external sensible object and constitutes a transition from potentiality to actuality through that object's agency, phantasia operates even when perception has ceased—in sleep, in recollection, in deliberation. The image-making faculty is thus grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception, causally derived from actual sensation as a κίνησις (movement) that persists beyond the perceptual encounter, yet it cannot be collapsed back into sensation precisely because it functions in the absence of the sensible particular. Accordingly, Caston argues that phantasia can be false, noting that Aristotle "says that a scene-painting or a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of'" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). This susceptibility to falsity further differentiates phantasia from veridical perception of proper sensibles. The internal distinction between sensitive phantasia (φαντασία αἰσθητική) and deliberative phantasia (φαντασία βουλευτική), which Papachristou treats at length, will be developed more fully in subsequent sections; here it suffices even at the most basic sensory grade, phantasia already exceeds mere sensation by introducing the possibility of error and voluntary image-formation (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7). 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The relationship between φαντασία as a capacity and the φάντασμα as its product is essential to understanding how Aristotle accounts for cognition beyond immediate perception. The phantasma is the quasi-perceptual content that persists after sensation ceases—an image or appearance retained in the soul, which serves as the medium through which higher cognitive operations, including thinking itself, proceed. Indeed, the canonical Aristotelian formula that the soul never thinks without a phantasma (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43) underscores the indispensability of image-content for both theoretical and practical intellect. Aristotle thereby establishes that phantasmata are not mere epiphenomenal residues of perception but rather constitutive elements of thought; hence phantasia, the movement that generates them, occupies a structurally necessary position in the economy of the soul. Caston emphasizes that this account introduces a mode of intentionality distinct from sensation, one that "makes error possible" and requires "its content to be explained in a different way" than the content of veridical perception (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, p. 18). Thus the phantasma carries representational content that can diverge from the actual state of affairs—a feature crucial for both sensitive and deliberative phantasia. The deliberative grade of phantasia, available only to rational animals, involves the voluntary manipulation and comparison of phantasmata in view of future action, whereas the sensitive grade produces phantasmata more directly tethered to prior perceptual encounters (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 20–22). Importantly, some non-rational animals possess phantasia without possessing rational discourse (λόγος) confirms that the production of phantasmata is not dependent upon belief (δόξα) or discursive reasoning; rather, the phantasma functions as a pre-linguistic form of cognitive content available even to creatures lacking the capacity for λόγος (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43; Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 46). 

## 3. Memory, Aristotle contends, always implies an elapsed time; accordingly, "only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). This passage reveals that the phantasma functioning as a memory-image bears a dual reference: it presents a content—an appearance of something previously perceived—while simultaneously marking that content as belonging to the past. Memory thus presupposes phantasia insofar as the remembered content is a phantasma, yet it contrasts with phantasia in its essential temporal determination; phantasia as such can generate images without any necessary orientation toward the past, as occurs in dreams, anticipation, or deliberation. The voluntariness of phantasia further distinguishes it from memory, since one may summon an image at will without thereby remembering, while genuine recollection involves a directed search through chains of residual movements (κινήσεις) preserved from prior perceptual experience. "one must cognize magnitude and motion by means of the same faculty by which one cognizes time" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1) situates the perception of temporal intervals within the broader perceptual apparatus that phantasia presupposes. White's observation that phantasia occupies the juncture between sensation and intellect helps clarify why memory cannot be assimilated to either pure perception or pure thought: it depends upon the phantasma's capacity to retain sensory content in an intellectually accessible form (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). The deliberative grade of phantasia, as Papachristou distinguishes it, extends this temporal orientation toward the future, enabling the rational animal to compare phantasmata of possible actions and their consequences—a function that memory's backward-looking temporality cannot perform (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 10–12). 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The distinction between phantasia and δόξα (belief or opinion) constitutes one of Aristotle's most careful delimitations in *De Anima* III.3, for while both phantasia and doxa involve representational content that can be true or false, they differ fundamentally in their relation to conviction and rational commitment. Aristotle insists that phantasia is not identical with any combination of opinion and perception, precisely because phantasmata may appear to us without our assenting to them—one may entertain an image of something fearful without believing oneself to be in danger, as occurs when we know the sun to be larger than the earth yet it appears (φαίνεται) to be a foot across (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). Doxa, by contrast, necessarily involves conviction (πίστις); to hold an opinion is to be persuaded of something, and persuasion requires λόγος. (Aristotle 2014, *Rhetoric*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in the *Movement of Animals*, "thinking and imagination produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement of Animals*, p. 11)—yet thinking here operates through conviction in a way that imagination need not. Caston underscores the philosophical stakes of this distinction: phantasia introduces a species of intentionality in which error is structurally possible without the commitment characteristic of belief, thereby filling a gap that neither sensation nor opinion alone can occupy (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4). The relation between phantasia and doxa is thus one of explanation rather than identity: phantasia provides the image-content upon which belief may supervene, but the formation of belief requires additional rational operations unavailable to non-rational animals. O'Gorman extends this analysis into the domain of rhetoric, arguing that "De Anima's discussion of phantasia illuminates Aristotle's ambivalence toward lexis in Rhetoric book 3 because phantasia, while integral to cognition, is vulnerable to distortion and error" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5). The voluntariness of phantasia—the capacity to summon images "before the eyes" (πρὸ ὀμμάτων ποιεῖν)—renders it a powerful instrument of persuasion and deliberation alike, yet this same voluntariness means that phantasia can generate appearances detached from truthful doxa, a tension that Aristotle never fully resolves and that reverberates through his accounts of practical reasoning and rhetorical reception.
